newsitem.title: USA: Few Americans understand public health - poll.
newsitem.headline: Few Americans understand public health - poll.

text.p: Almost all Americans believe public health programmes are important but few understand that they focus on preventing disease and promoting health, according to an opinion poll released Monday.

The Harris Poll found that only 1 percent of respondents said public health concerned health education or healthier lifestyles, only 1 percent answered that public health related to the prevention of infectious diseases and just 1 percent said it involved immunisation.

"While the nation's leading medical schools are highly visible, schools of public health, often in the same universities, are relatively unknown," said Humphrey Taylor, chairman and CEO of Louis Harris and Associates Inc, which conducted the survey.

"However, it is generally accepted that the major increases in life expectancy which have occurred throughout the world in this century are mainly the result of improvements in public health rather than improvements in the treatment of disease," Humphrey said.
The poll was conducted by telephone in the United States between Dec. 12 and 16, 1996, among 1,004 adults. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

It found that 93 percent of Americans believe that the prevention and spread of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis, measles, flu and AIDS -- one important function of public health -- is "very important".
Some 82 percent believe that ensuring people are not exposed to unsafe water, air pollution or toxic waste is also "very important" -- another function of government public heatlh programmes.

Surveyors said that when the meaning of public health was explained to respondents, 57 percent said public health should be a government responsibility, with more people naming the federal government rather than state or local government.
Criticism and public pressure for major changes in the U.S. health care system have increased sharply since early 1996, according to the Harris Poll.

It revealed that those who think "the system works pretty well" are down to 11 percent and those who believe "we need to completely rebuild the system" rose to 35 percent from 24 percent in January 1996.
"Indeed, attitudes to the health care system are as hostile now as they were in 1993 before Bill and Hillary Clinton's ill-fated proposal for health care reform," Humphrey said.
